items.followUp: Using a velocity–time graph, derive the relation 2aS = Vf² − Vi².

rubric.why: The area under the velocity–time graph gives displacement.
rubric.description: Uses the trapezium area to express displacement.
rubric.how: Award for stating the trapezium-area relation between S, Vi, Vf and t.

rubric.why: The slope of the velocity–time graph gives acceleration.
rubric.description: Expresses acceleration as the graph’s gradient.
rubric.how: Award for writing the acceleration relation from the slope.

rubric.why: Combining the two relations produces the required product.
rubric.description: Substitutes the acceleration relation into the displacement relation.
rubric.how: Award for the correct intermediate equation.

rubric.why: This is the required result after using difference of squares.
rubric.how: Award for the correctly simplified final equation.

modelAnswer: From the velocity–time graph, displacement S is the area of the trapezium.
S = 1/2 (Vi + Vf)t
The slope of the velocity–time graph gives acceleration: a = (Vf − Vi)/t.
Therefore, t = (Vf − Vi)/a.
Substituting in the displacement equation: S = (Vi + Vf)(Vf − Vi)/(2a).
Multiplying both sides by 2a: 2aS = (Vf − Vi)(Vf + Vi).
Using (x − y)(x + y) = x² − y²: 2aS = Vf² − Vi².

items.followUp: Define equilibrium and state the second condition of equilibrium.

rubric.why: Equilibrium describes a body whose state of rest or uniform motion does not change.
rubric.how: Award for defining equilibrium as a state in which a body remains at rest or moves with constant velocity.

rubric.why: The first condition is the zero-resultant-force condition.
rubric.description: States the first condition of equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award for the vector sum/resultant of all forces being zero.

rubric.why: Zero resultant force means no change in translational motion.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that forces balance and there is no acceleration.

modelAnswer: A body is in equilibrium if it remains at rest or moves with constant velocity.
First condition of equilibrium: the vector sum of all forces acting on a body must be zero, ΣF = 0.
This means the forces are balanced and the body has no acceleration; it is in translational equilibrium.

items.followUp: A motor gives 180 J of useful output energy from 600 J of input energy. Calculate its efficiency as a percentage.

rubric.why: Correctly identifies the useful work and total input energy.
rubric.description: States the given data in SI units.
rubric.how: Award for identifying 12 J useful work and 100 J input energy.

rubric.why: Efficiency is the ratio of useful output to input, expressed as a percentage.
rubric.how: Award for the correct percentage formula.

rubric.why: Substitution must use the given values in the correct order.
rubric.description: Substitutes the given values with units.
rubric.how: Award for correctly substituting 12 J and 100 J.

rubric.why: The calculation gives an efficiency of 0.12, or 12 percent.
rubric.how: Award one mark for the correct numerical calculation and one for the final answer with the percent sign.

modelAnswer: Given: useful work = 12 J; food energy input = 100 J.
Formula: Efficiency = (useful work / input energy) × 100%.
Substitution: Efficiency = (12 J / 100 J) × 100%.
Efficiency = 12%.

items.followUp: Define a physical quantity and write the general form of a number in scientific notation.

rubric.why: A physical quantity is measurable and is expressed by a magnitude and unit.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a physical quantity can be measured and expressed with a magnitude and unit.

rubric.why: Scientific notation expresses a number as a coefficient times a power of ten, with a coefficient from 1 up to but not including 10.
rubric.how: Award for the general form and the required range of the coefficient.

modelAnswer: A physical quantity is a quantity that can be measured and expressed by a numerical value (magnitude) and a unit.
Scientific notation expresses a number in the form a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n is an integer.

items.followUp: Name two important parts of a micrometer screw gauge.

rubric.why: The main scale is one of the principal scales of a vernier calipers.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the main scale.

rubric.why: The vernier scale is the other principal scale.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the vernier scale.

modelAnswer: Two important parts of vernier calipers are the main scale and the vernier scale.

items.followUp: Define speed and state what acceleration measures.

accept: change in position per unit time
rubric.why: Velocity describes displacement per unit time and has direction.
rubric.how: Award for defining velocity as displacement per unit time, with direction.

accept: change in velocity per unit time
rubric.why: Acceleration measures how quickly velocity changes with time.
rubric.how: Award for the rate-of-change-of-velocity definition.

modelAnswer: Velocity is the displacement of a body per unit time in a specified direction.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time.

items.followUp: Draw a distance–time graph for a body moving at a constant speed of 3 m/s for 4 s.

rubric.why: The distance–time graph must have correctly labelled axes.
rubric.how: Award for time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis, with suitable units.

rubric.why: At constant speed, distance increases uniformly with time, giving a straight line.
rubric.description: Plots appropriate points and draws the constant-speed graph.
rubric.how: Award for a straight line with uniform slope through the plotted values; equivalent values for any constant speed are acceptable.

modelAnswer: Use a distance–time graph: horizontal axis = time t (s); vertical axis = distance d (m).
Table of values: t (s): 0, 1, 2, 3; d (m): 0, 2, 4, 6 (constant speed = 2 m/s).
Plot the points (0 s, 0 m), (1 s, 2 m), (2 s, 4 m), and (3 s, 6 m).
Join the points with a straight line through the origin; its constant slope represents constant speed.

items.followUp: What is friction? Explain why rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction.

rubric.why: Friction acts between surfaces in contact and opposes their relative motion or tendency to move.
rubric.how: Award for stating that friction opposes relative motion between surfaces in contact.

rubric.why: Rolling involves less interlocking or deformation of surfaces than sliding, so the resisting force is smaller.
rubric.description: Explains why rolling friction is less.
rubric.how: Award for linking the lower rolling resistance to less interlocking, deformation, or contact compared with sliding.

modelAnswer: Friction is the force that opposes the relative motion, or tendency of motion, between surfaces in contact.
Rolling friction is less than sliding friction because, during rolling, the surfaces interlock or deform less than when one surface slides over another.
